A Tour of the kinvicalc Shiny App

kinvicalc_app_tour.Rmd

Who this vignette is for

kinvicalc ships with a Shiny app (run_app()) that lets a lab operator record kinematic viscosity measurements, check them against ASTM D445-26 precision limits, and maintain a registry of viscometers, all without writing any R code. This vignette walks through the app screen by screen, following one sample from an empty registry through to a locked, reportable result. It complements the updating_precision_values vignette, which covers changing the ASTM limits the app checks against, and the kinvicalc-workflows vignette, which shows the same workflow driven from R directly.

Launch the app from an R console with:

library(kinvicalc)
run_app()

This opens in your default web browser (or the Viewer pane in RStudio/ Positron). The app has three tabs: Calculation, Reporting, and Viscometers. The tour below visits them in the order a new lab would typically use them: register a viscometer first, then run and lock a sample result, then review the locked results table.

Step 1: Register a viscometer

Before any sample can be measured, the viscometer used for the test must be in the local registry. Open the Viscometers tab. On a fresh installation, the maintenance form and the results table below it are both empty:

The Viscometers tab before any viscometer has been added.

Fill in the viscometer’s size, serial number, and its four calibration factors (top and bottom bulb, at 40 C and 100 C, taken from the viscometer’s certificate). As you type the size and serial number, the app previews the canonical NNN-NNNNN viscometer ID it will use as the primary key:

Filling in a new viscometer’s size, serial number, and calibration factors. The Viscometer ID preview updates live above the “Added by” field.

Clicking Add to registry stores the viscometer and immediately reflects it in the table at the bottom of the tab, along with an entry timestamp and a use counter that starts at zero:

The viscometer now appears in the registry table, with entry date and a use counter.

If you instead enter a size/serial combination that already exists, this same button relabels itself Update Viscometer Factors and pops a confirmation dialog before correcting the stored factors – this is the supported way to fix a data-entry error in a calibration factor without losing the viscometer’s creation date or use history. The lower half of this tab also has controls for marking a viscometer cleaned (resetting its use-since-cleaning counter), archiving a retired viscometer, and unarchiving one if needed.

Step 2: Enter a sample and check the result

Switch to the Calculation tab. Before anything is entered, the form shows a placeholder result and a reminder of which fields are still needed:

The Calculation tab with no inputs yet. The result panel shows “No result yet” and the message strip lists the required fields.

Fill in the operator’s user ID, a sample ID, the viscometer to use (chosen from the registry populated in Step 1), the sample type, the analysis temperature, and the two measured flow times. The result panel on the right updates live as you type – there is no separate “Calculate” button. Here, both flow times are close enough together that the determinability check (ASTM D445-26 11.2.3/12.4.1, comparing the two individually calculated viscosities) passes:

Both flow times entered. The result panel shows both calculated viscosities and a PASS determinability check.

Had the two flow times disagreed by more than the sample type’s determinability limit, this panel would instead show FAIL in red and the message strip below the result panel would recommend cleaning and redrying the viscometer before repeating the measurement, per ASTM D445-26 11.2.3/12.4.1 – the app surfaces this as a warning rather than blocking the result outright, since the operator may still need to record and investigate a failing pair.

Standard reference-sample QA/QC

Selecting sample type Standard Reference Material reveals an additional required field, Expected Value, and unlocks two more checks once it is filled in: a repeatability (r) and reproducibility (R) comparison of the measured result against that known expected value, per the lab’s Characterization Laboratory QA/QC procedure. Unlike the ordinary repeatability/reproducibility checks (which compare two independent measured results and center the limit on their average), this standard check centers the limit on the expected value itself:

Selecting “Standard Reference Material” adds an Expected Value field and shows repeatability and reproducibility pass/fail checks centered on that value.

Step 3: Lock the result

Once you are satisfied with the calculated result, click Lock result. Locking clears the sample ID and flow-time fields (ready for the next sample on the same viscometer) and confirms the sample name that was just locked:

After locking, the result panel resets and a confirmation message names the locked sample.

Locking also increments the viscometer’s use counter in the registry, so the Viscometers tab’s “Uses Since Clean” column stays current without a separate manual step.

Step 4: Review locked results

The Reporting tab accumulates every result locked during the current app session into a single table, formatted for a QA record: sample identity, viscometer, both individual flow times and viscosities, the averaged result, a colour-coded QA/QC column, and the operator and timestamp:

The Reporting tab’s locked-results table after one sample has been locked.

For a standard reference sample, the QA/QC column shows three lines (determinability, r, and R) instead of the single determinability line shown for other sample types, so a reviewer can see all three checks at a glance without opening each row’s original calculation.

Summary

The app tour follows one path through kinvicalc’s three tabs: register a viscometer (Viscometers), enter and lock a sample result while reviewing its precision checks (Calculation), and review the accumulated, reportable results for the session (Reporting). The underlying calculations, precision rules, and registry are exactly the functions documented in the package’s other vignettes and help pages – the app is a convenience layer over build_sample_result(), add_viscometer(), update_viscometer_factors(), and the rest of the exported API, for operators who prefer a form-based workflow to writing R code directly.

Appendix: viscometer maintenance actions

Section Step 1 above covers adding a brand-new viscometer. The same Viscometers tab also supports three ongoing maintenance actions on a viscometer already in the registry: correcting its calibration factors, marking it as cleaned, and taking it in and out of service via archiving. This appendix walks through each.

Correcting calibration factors

If a calibration factor was mistyped, or the viscometer has been re-certified with new factors, re-enter that viscometer’s size and serial number in the same form used to add it. As soon as the size/serial combination matches an existing registry entry, the action button relabels itself Update Viscometer Factors in place of Add to registry:

Re-entering an existing viscometer’s size and serial number relabels the action button “Update Viscometer Factors”. Here factor_40_top is being corrected from 0.03450 to 0.03448, with a note explaining the change.

Clicking it pops a confirmation dialog before anything is written, since this action overwrites the stored factors:

The confirmation dialog for a viscometer factor update.

Confirming applies the new factors and records the note. Only the four calibration factors and the notes field are changed – the registry preserves the original entry date and use counters, so the viscometer’s history stays intact:

After confirming, the registry table shows the corrected factor and the note, while the entry date and use counter are unchanged from before the correction.

If you leave Notes blank when correcting factors, kinvicalc writes an auto-generated "Updated <date> by <updated_by>" note instead, so a correction is never left untraceable.

Marking a viscometer cleaned

ASTM D445-26 calls for periodic deep cleaning of a viscometer, and the “Uses Since Clean” count in the registry table tracks how many measurements have accumulated since the last clean. Select the viscometer from the Viscometer ID to mark clean dropdown and click Mark cleaning to reset that counter and stamp a new “Last Clean Date”:

Marking viscometer 200-00123 as cleaned resets its use counter to zero and stamps today’s date as the Last Clean Date.

Archiving and unarchiving a viscometer

When a viscometer is retired or taken out of service (for example, damaged or sent out for re-certification), archive it using the Viscometer ID to archive dropdown and Archive viscometer button. Archiving does not delete the viscometer or its history – it only removes it from the active selection lists used elsewhere in the app (such as the Calculation tab’s viscometer dropdown), and it becomes available in the Viscometer ID to unarchive dropdown instead:

After archiving, viscometer 200-00123 no longer appears in the “to archive” dropdown but does appear, tagged [archived], in the “to unarchive” dropdown.

To bring it back into service, select it from Viscometer ID to unarchive and click Unarchive viscometer. This clears the archived status and returns the viscometer to the active dropdowns used for new measurements:

Unarchiving viscometer 200-00123 returns it to active status.

Appendix: standard reference materials and automated pass/fail

Section Standard reference-sample QA/QC above introduces the Standard Reference Material sample type and its Expected Value field. This appendix follows a standard reference sample all the way through to a locked, reported result, and then shows what a failing check looks like, so the two cases can be compared directly.

A standard reference material is a substance with a known, certified kinematic viscosity (an “expected value”) used to verify that a viscometer, operator, and procedure are all performing within the Characterization Laboratory’s QA/QC tolerances – rather than checking one sample’s internal consistency, it checks the whole measurement process against a trusted external answer. Because that answer is known in advance, kinvicalc can automatically calculate whether the measured result agrees with it closely enough, without the operator needing to look anything up.

Locking and reporting a passing standard check

Continuing from the passing repeatability/reproducibility check shown earlier, click Lock result just as with any other sample:

After locking a standard reference sample, the result panel resets and confirms the locked sample name – the same behaviour as locking any other sample type.

On the Reporting tab, the standard reference sample’s QA/QC column shows three pass/fail lines instead of the single determinability line shown for an ordinary sample, so a reviewer can confirm at a glance that the viscometer and procedure are in control:

The Reporting tab with both an ordinary sample (single “Determ” line) and a standard reference sample (three lines: Determ, r, and R) locked in the same session.

What a failing standard check looks like

The repeatability and reproducibility limits scale with the expected value, so entering an expected value that disagrees substantially with the measured result – for example, from a mislabeled reference standard, or a viscometer drifting out of calibration – produces an automatic FAIL on both checks, shown in red exactly like a failing determinability check:

An expected value of 8.50 mm²/s against a measured result of about 7.44 mm²/s produces a large repeatability/reproducibility difference, and both checks are automatically marked FAIL.

Note that determinability still passed here (the two flow times agree with each other), since it measures a different thing: determinability compares the sample’s own two determinations to each other, while the repeatability and reproducibility checks compare the measured result to the known expected value. A standard reference sample can fail one without the other, and reviewing all three lines together is what makes the distinction visible on the Reporting tab.
